question: Moving rack power distribution from about 54 volts to 800 volts saves copper and cuts heat loss mainly because of what change?

options.A: Copper resists electricity far less at higher voltage
options.B: Direct current produces no heat in a conductor
options.C: Equal power flows with about one fifteenth the current
options.D: Each rack draws much less total power than before

rationales.A: The lesson ties the savings to lower current. A conductor's resistance does not drop because the voltage is higher.
rationales.B: Heat loss in any conductor rises with the square of the current, so direct current still loses heat.
rationales.C: Power equals voltage times current, so at 800 volts the same power needs roughly a fifteenth of the current, which allows thinner conductors and much lower losses since loss scales with current squared.
rationales.D: Racks are drawing more power, up to one megawatt. The voltage change delivers that same power with less current.

wrong_choice_note: A is most tempting because it sounds like a property of high voltage. The real lever is current: less current means thinner copper and losses that fall with the square of the current.
source_excerpt: Raising the voltage lets the same power flow with a fraction of the current. Moving from about 54 volts to 800 volts cuts the current for a given power by roughly a factor of fifteen.

question: Under the Mount Diablo specification from Google, Meta and Microsoft, where does power conversion equipment go for racks drawing 100 kilowatts to one megawatt?

options.A: Inside each server, as in older AC designs
options.B: Out at the utility substation beyond the site
options.C: Into battery cabinets mounted under the floor
options.D: Into a separate sidecar rack beside the compute

rationales.A: Conversion inside each server is the older approach that worked for low-power racks. Mount Diablo moves it out because at these power levels it crowds out computing equipment.
rationales.B: The utility substation is far upstream. Mount Diablo places conversion right next to the computing rack.
rationales.C: The lesson does not describe batteries as part of Mount Diablo. Conversion goes into a dedicated power rack.
rationales.D: Mount Diablo disaggregates the rack: a sidecar power rack does the conversion and feeds the computing rack at high-voltage DC, freeing space for more accelerators.

wrong_choice_note: A is most tempting because it describes how racks were powered for most of the industry's history. The lesson's point is that at 100 kilowatts and above, that in-rack power gear takes space the accelerators need.
source_excerpt: Power conversion moves out of the server rack into a separate sidecar power rack, which feeds the computing rack at high voltage direct current, either plus or minus 400 volts or 800 volts.

question: Why is it harder to interrupt a fault on an 800-volt DC circuit than on an AC circuit?

options.A: It lacks the zero crossing that helps breakers quench an arc
options.B: It always carries far more current at the same voltage level
options.C: Its breakers must wait for the utility to cut medium voltage
options.D: Its arcs can only form inside the solid-state transformers

rationales.A: AC passes through zero volts many times a second, which helps a breaker extinguish the arc when a circuit opens. DC stays at full voltage, so breaking a DC fault needs different equipment.
rationales.B: At the same voltage and power, current is the same for AC and DC. The difficulty comes from the missing zero crossing.
rationales.C: The difficulty sits at the breaker itself: with no zero crossing, a DC arc gets no natural help to go out, so the circuit needs different protective equipment. Nothing upstream at the utility is involved.
rationales.D: An arc forms wherever a circuit opens under load. The lesson does not limit DC arcs to solid-state transformers.

wrong_choice_note: B is most tempting because the lesson links high current to problems elsewhere. The safety issue for DC is specific: with no zero crossing, the arc does not get the natural help AC gives a breaker.
source_excerpt: Alternating current, or AC, passes through zero volts many times a second, which helps circuit breakers extinguish the arc that forms when a circuit opens; direct current, or DC, does not, so breaking a DC fault is harder and needs different equipment.
